pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Plants Grow from Air & Water (mass comes from air/water, not soil)

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-LS1-1):** '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1].' [Clarif: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1].] DCI LS1.C: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1].' The named practice is ARGUE FROM EVIDENCE — the whole topic is building a case against intuition.

- **Standards — UK (DfE):** KS2 doesn't state the air/water-mass claim explicitly; it bridges Y3 plant requirements to KS3 photosynthesis ('plants make carbohydrates in leaves... obtaining water and mineral ions from soil, CO2 from air'). This topic is chiefly NGSS-anchored.

- **Operational details:** This is a COUNTERINTUITIVE claim that must be won with EVIDENCE, because every child's intuition says a plant's stuff comes from the soil it's rooted in ('plants eat soil'). The decisive evidence is the classic mass-balance argument (van Helmont's willow): a tree can gain many kilograms over years while the soil it grows in loses only grams — so the mass did NOT come from the soil; it came from something invisible taken from the AIR (carbon dioxide) plus WATER. The teaching sequence: surface the intuition → confront it with the soil-barely-changed data → reason that the gained mass must come from air + water — that IS the argument NGSS wants. Soil minerals matter (health), but are a tiny fraction of mass, not the bulk material. This directly demolishes the domain's most durable plant misconception and sets up photosynthesis (where the air's CO2 and water become the plant's sugars/structure). Keep the mechanism light at KS2/grade-5 (materials from air and water); the CO2→glucose chemistry is KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal — argument from evidence against intuition). Given data that a growing plant gains large mass while its soil mass barely changes, the child constructs the argument that the material came chiefly from air and water rather than soil, explicitly rejecting 'plants get their mass/food from soil'.
bestPractices: Elicit the intuition first ('where does a giant tree's wood come from?') so the evidence has a misconception to overturn — confronting the prior idea is essential.
Anchor on the mass-balance evidence (van Helmont-style): plant gains kilograms, soil loses only grams → the mass can't be from soil → it's from air + water.
Teach it AS an argument from evidence (the NGSS practice): claim + the soil-unchanged data + reasoning, not as a fact to accept.
Separate minerals (small amounts, for health, from soil) from the BULK material (air's CO2 + water) so 'nutrients from soil' isn't overstated.
Bridge forward to photosynthesis lightly — the invisible air gas plus water become the plant's food/structure — without the KS3 equation.
Use the surprise deliberately: the invisibility of air-as-material is what makes soil feel like the obvious (wrong) source.
keyRepresentations: A before/after mass-balance: potted sapling + weighed soil → years later, heavy tree + almost-unchanged soil.
A twin-pan balance contrasting grams-of-soil-lost vs kilograms-of-plant-gained.
An arrow model: CO2 (from air) + water (from soil) → plant material, with soil minerals as a thin side-arrow.
A claim–evidence–reasoning frame built around the soil-unchanged data.
commonMisconceptions: 'Plants get their food/mass from the soil' — the dominant, tenacious misconception this topic exists to demolish.
Believing a plant's wood/mass comes mostly from water alone, omitting the air (CO2) contribution.
Thinking air can't be 'material' because it's invisible and weightless (so it couldn't build a tree).
Assuming soil minerals are the plant's food rather than small quantities for health.
Confusing where WATER comes from (soil) with where the bulk MATERIAL comes from (air + water) — conceding water-from-soil then wrongly extending to all mass.
Treating the claim as something to memorise rather than something the mass-balance evidence proves.

learn.summary: For ages 10-11: build the argument that most of a plant's growing mass comes from air (carbon dioxide) and water, not from the soil it grows in. The whole topic is an argument-from-evidence against the durable 'plants eat soil' intuition, anchored on the classic mass-balance (van Helmont) evidence: a plant gains kilograms while its soil loses only grams. Keep the mechanism light at this level (materials come from air and water); the CO2 to glucose chemistry belongs to a later stage.

activities.title: Where does a tree come from? A mass-balance investigation
feedback: If you chose 'soil' as the source: look again at the two numbers. The soil lost only ~57 g but the plant gained ~75 kg - that's over a thousand times more. The soil simply did not lose enough mass to have become the tree.

If you credited water only and left out air: that was van Helmont's own conclusion, and the weighing alone can't rule it out. But water contains no carbon, while dry wood and leaves are roughly half carbon by mass. Carbon dioxide from the air carries that carbon into the wood and leaves, so both air and water are sources.

If you worried that 'air weighs nothing so it can't build a tree': air and the gases in it do have mass; the carbon dioxide taken in over years supplies carbon that becomes real solid material. Its invisibility is exactly why soil feels like the obvious (but wrong) answer.
Strong answer: you located the mass in air (CO2) + water AND used the barely-changed soil as the evidence that rules soil out.
activities.rationale: Eliciting the intuition first gives the evidence a misconception to overturn, and the mass-balance contrast (kilograms gained vs grams lost) generates the surprising numbers the NGSS argue-from-evidence practice requires. Letting the learner propose 'soil' and watch the numbers refuse it is intended to make the reasoning more memorable than presenting the conclusion pre-drawn, though this comparative effect is not established by the sources.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-LS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1]'; clarification: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1] soil; DCI LS1.C '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1].'
'Plants get their food/mass from the soil' is the dominant and most durable plant-biology misconception; the mass-balance (van Helmont) argument is the classic evidence used to overturn it.
learnerActions: First, before any data, answer aloud or in writing: 'A tiny sapling grows into a huge tree weighing tens of kilograms. Where did all that extra wood and leaf material come from?' Record your honest prediction (most learners say 'from the soil').
Record starting masses: a pot of dried soil (e.g. 90.000 kg) and a tiny sapling (e.g. 2 kg).

Over the growing period, add nothing to the pot but water, and cover the soil so dust or fallen leaves can't change its mass. Then re-weigh both the grown plant and the soil, drying the soil again first so that differences in how wet it is don't hide the result (e.g. tree now 77 kg; soil now 89.943 kg).
Compute and compare the two changes side by side: plant gained about +75 kg; soil lost only about 57 g (-0.057 kg).
Try to answer 'where did the ~75 kg come from?' by proposing soil as the source, then test that idea against the numbers: the soil barely changed, so it cannot account for ~75 kg.

Reveal and state the source: invisible carbon dioxide taken from the air, plus water. Note that the weighing rules out soil but cannot by itself tell air from water (van Helmont himself concluded the mass came from water). The extra clue is that much of a plant's dry material is carbon, which carbon dioxide contains and water does not. Write a claim-evidence-reasoning statement: CLAIM (mass comes chiefly from air and water); EVIDENCE (plant +75 kg while soil only -57 g; plant material contains carbon, and carbon dioxide in the air is the carbon source); REASONING (if the soil had supplied the mass it would have lost kilograms, so the mass came from elsewhere; the other inputs were water and air, and the carbon must have come from the air).
activities.intendedInsight: A growing plant gains far more mass than the soil loses, so the soil cannot be the source of that mass. The weighing alone doesn't separate air from water, but the carbon in plant material shows that carbon dioxide from the air contributes along with water. This is an argument from evidence, not a fact to memorise.

activities.title: Simulated mass-balance with live readouts (optional interactive version)
feedback: Dragging 'soil' in and seeing the numbers reject it is the key moment - note why: the soil mass hardly changed.
After revealing air + water, re-state the argument in your own words rather than just reading the panel.
activities.rationale: The real experiment takes years; a fast simulation can run it in seconds and put both masses on one balance so the learner sees the gap directly. The live readouts, source-dragging and reveal toggle are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required features, and whether the simulation is more effective than other media is not established.
learnerActions: On a digital scale, weigh the soil and sapling to set starting values.
Drag a time slider across several years while adding only water; watch the sapling grow into a substantial tree.
Re-weigh everything; two readouts animate side by side - e.g. TREE +75 kg vs SOIL -57 g.
Respond to the prompt 'where did the mass come from?' by dragging a candidate source (soil / air / water) into the balance; a 'soil' choice is refuted because the soil readout barely moved.
Toggle to reveal carbon dioxide (from air) + water as the material, then assemble the claim-evidence-reasoning panel.
activities.intendedInsight: Compressing a years-long experiment into seconds is intended to let the learner personally generate and confront the kilograms-gained-versus-grams-lost gap, so the air+water conclusion can land as a genuine surprise.

activities.title: Defend the claim against a skeptic
feedback: On the gas challenge: explain that air and CO2 have mass and the carbon in CO2 becomes part of the plant's solid body over time.
On the plant-food challenge: fertiliser supplies small amounts of minerals for health, not the bulk material; the bulk comes from CO2 and water. Distinguish minerals from mass.
Credit arguments that cite the barely-changed soil as evidence, not just assertions of the correct answer.
activities.rationale: Because the target practice is argue-from-evidence against a strong intuition, a Socratic exchange is intended to exercise the child's reasoning and can surface the misconception; it supports the investigation rather than replacing it, since without the mass figures in front of them the evidence is weaker.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-LS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1]'; clarification: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1] soil; DCI LS1.C '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS1-1].'
learnerActions: Face a skeptical partner (or role-play one) who insists 'the tree's wood obviously came from the soil it grew in - convince me otherwise.'
Marshal the mass-balance evidence out loud: state the figures (plant +kg, soil -grams) and reason that the soil could not be the source.
Respond to follow-up challenges: 'Carbon dioxide is a gas - how can a gas become solid wood?' and 'A gardener adds plant food to the pot - isn't that where the mass comes from?'
Keep arguing until the skeptic concedes only to sound reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Defending the claim aloud - not just recognising the right answer - rehearses the argue-from-evidence practice and can surface any residual 'soil' or 'water-only' thinking.

activities.title: Separate the minerals from the mass; bridge to photosynthesis
feedback: Watch the common slip: conceding 'water comes from soil' and then wrongly extending it to 'so all the mass comes from soil'. Water is from soil, but the carbon-carrying material is from the air.
If you labelled minerals as the plant's 'food', revise: minerals are small quantities for health; the bulk material is carbon, oxygen and hydrogen from CO2 and water.
activities.rationale: Best practice separates minerals (small, for health, from soil) from the bulk material (air's CO2 + water) so 'nutrients from soil' isn't overstated, and bridges forward to photosynthesis lightly. The CO2 to glucose chemistry is left for a later stage.
sourceClaims: DfE positions this between Y3 plant requirements and KS3 photosynthesis (leaves make carbohydrate from CO2 in air and water); the explicit air/water-mass claim is chiefly NGSS-anchored.
learnerActions: Draw an arrow model: CO2 (from air) + water (from soil) -> plant material, with soil minerals shown as a thin side-arrow.
Explain in a sentence the different jobs: water comes from the soil (and is a source of material); air supplies carbon dioxide; soil minerals come in small amounts for health, not bulk.
State the forward link lightly: the invisible air gas plus water become the plant's food and structure (this is photosynthesis), without writing any chemical equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Water coming from the soil does not mean all the mass comes from the soil; minerals are a tiny health contribution, and the bulk material is CO2 + water. This sets up photosynthesis without overreaching the mechanism.

constraints: This is a counterintuitive claim that must be won with evidence; elicit the 'plants eat soil' intuition first so the mass-balance data has something to overturn.
Teach it as an argument from evidence (claim + soil-unchanged data + reasoning), not as a fact to accept or memorise.
Keep the mechanism light for this age: materials come from air and water. The CO2 to glucose chemistry and the balanced photosynthesis equation are for a later (KS3) stage.

Distinguish water taken up from the soil from material made of the soil itself: conceding that water comes from soil must not be extended to claiming all mass comes from soil. The bulk material is built from carbon dioxide from the air plus water.
Distinguish minerals/fertiliser (small amounts for health) from the bulk mass (carbon, oxygen, hydrogen from CO2 and water).

Multiple-choice and ordering tasks can present the evidence and check the argument, but recognition-format responses do not by themselves show the learner can independently construct and defend the argument; include a prediction and a written or spoken claim-evidence-reasoning step.
A pre-drawn reveal or a simulation shows or compresses the experiment; prefer having the learner predict first and confront the numbers themselves rather than reading a conclusion already drawn.

The specific simulation masses (90.000 kg soil, 2 kg sapling, 77 kg tree, 89.943 kg soil, +75 kg / -57 g) are illustrative figures for making the contrast vivid, not measured results from a particular real trial.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a 3D treatment as adding 'no evidential value' and framed the simulation as uniquely able to teach this. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; omitted/softened. A static before/after image or a debate can still support the argument, with the noted limit that they present rather than generate the surprising numbers.

Numeric self-check of the illustrative example: soil change 90.000 - 89.943 = 0.057 kg = 57 g lost; plant change 77 - 2 = 75 kg gained (about 1,300 times the soil loss). These are internally consistent and kept only as an illustration, not as data from a specific real experiment.

The OU OpenLearn misconception/van Helmont source is marked verified:false in the row; the claim that 'plants eat soil' is the dominant plant-biology misconception and that van Helmont is the classic counter-evidence is treated as legacy, unverified support, even where copied into an activity's sourceClaims.

At this age the chemistry of how CO2 and water become solid plant material is deliberately left unexplained; the point is the mass accounting, not the reaction mechanism. Avoid implying the mechanism has been taught.
Comparative efficacy of the simulation versus a debate or static image is not established; efficacy wording has been qualified as intended rather than demonstrated throughout the activities.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain (van Helmont): describe weighing a potted plant and its dried soil now and after a year of growth. Ask the child to predict how each mass changes, and WHY, before revealing the data. A 'plants eat soil' model predicts a large soil loss matching the plant's gain. The soil barely changes while the plant gains kilograms. The pre-observation reasoning about where mass comes from is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If the soil only lost a few grams, how can it be where the kilograms of plant came from?
Carbon dioxide is a gas — how can a gas end up as solid wood and leaves?
What job does the water do, and what job does the air do, in building the plant?
A gardener adds 'plant food' to the pot. Is that where the plant's mass comes from? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Most of the plant's mass comes from the AIR (carbon dioxide) and WATER, not from the soil. In photosynthesis the leaves use light to build food (and the plant's body) from CO₂ taken from the air and water — that's why a huge plant can grow while the soil barely changes. Full marks locate the mass in air+water and use the barely-changed soil as the evidence.

errorPatterns.pattern: plants eat the soil, so mass comes from soil ('the soil turns into plant')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Present the mass-balance data (plant +kg, soil −grams). The soil can't be the source — the mass came from air and water. This is the classic van Helmont result.
errorPatterns.distractor: The soil turned into the plant, so the soil lost kilograms of mass.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts the soil lost kilograms, or can't explain the barely-changed soil

errorPatterns.pattern: the mass came mostly from the water alone (air contributes nothing)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Air has mass and CO₂ carries carbon — the carbon in the plant's body comes from air. Both air and water are sources.
errorPatterns.distractor: It all came from the water — air can't add any weight.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: credits water but denies air/CO₂ can add solid mass ('air weighs nothing')

errorPatterns.pattern: fertiliser/plant food is the plant's actual food and mass source
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fertiliser supplies small amounts of minerals, not the bulk material — the bulk is carbon/oxygen/hydrogen from CO₂ and water. Distinguish minerals from mass.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the added 'plant food' built the plant's body

responseLevels.gap: Says the mass came from the soil (plants eat soil); can't reconcile the near-unchanged soil with the huge plant.
responseLevels.full: Argues most mass comes from air (CO₂) and water via photosynthesis, uses the barely-changed soil as evidence against 'plants eat soil', and distinguishes bulk mass from the small mineral contribution of fertiliser.
responseLevels.partial: Says the soil isn't the main source and names water, but omits air/CO₂ or can't use the mass-balance evidence — the idea without the full air-and-water argument.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A tiny seedling is planted in a pot of soil and grows over years into a huge plant weighing many kilograms. If I weighed the soil at the start and again years later, the soil would have lost only a few grams. So where did all the plant's extra mass come from? Explain your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason is the van Helmont discriminator: a child who understands plants build mass from air and water reconciles the huge plant with the near-unchanged soil; a child holding 'plants eat soil' cannot — they predict the soil should have lost kilograms.
